title_en: Chapter 13: The Threshold That Held No One
title_vi: Chương 13: Ngưỡng Cửa Không Giữ Người
content_en:
The sword-mark vanished before the light around it had time to cool.

Michael stood before the Boundary Gate, his right hand open upon the metal plate that had once received his authority. The engravings remained: seven rings nested within one another, a straight axis passing through their center, the sign of the one permitted to open a path when two realms drew too near. But the light had left them. The plate had not gone dark; it simply no longer recognized him.

Gabriel stood across the ritual circle, his staff upright before his chest. Three bands of script revolved around its head, slow and even, like blades that had not yet chosen where to fall.

Healiangel stood between them.

No one had asked him to.

Michael placed a finger upon the outermost ring. Nothing answered.

“Final confirmation,” Gabriel said. “Your boundary authority has been withdrawn from the entire Humanity record branch. The rights to open deeply, compel an image, force a response, and close a feedback path no longer recognize your mark.”

“I know.”

“You cannot restore them yourself.”

“I know.”

“The Council asks whether you request the opening of a restoration rite.”

Michael looked at the metal plate. A minute indentation remained where he had laid the edge of his sword upon the sign of authority. Not a fracture. Not damage. Only proof that a power once seated there had been removed by the hand that bore it.

“No.”

The three bands of script around Gabriel’s staff stopped at once.

“Without a request for restoration, the Humanity branch will have no unilateral keeper of the boundary.”

“It still retains the minimum danger warning.”

“A warning is not action.”

“Action is not always a right.”

Gabriel looked directly at him. “When something crosses and we cannot close it, that sentence will preserve no one.”

Michael closed his hand.

“When that happens, I will bear my share.”

“You have just abandoned the tool that would help you avoid bearing it.”

“No.” Michael turned away from the metal plate. “I abandoned the tool that allowed me to make another bear it in my place.”

The hollow beneath Healiangel’s left wing tightened. He had felt the downward thread fall silent when the rite ended, but it had not vanished. It remained like a shape remembered within his being—unlit, uncalling, leading nowhere he had the right to name.

Gabriel lowered his staff.

“I will record: restoration declined.”

“Record what happened.”

“That is what happened.”

“No.” Michael looked at him. “I am not refusing responsibility. I am refusing to reclaim that power before Heaven knows whom it is protecting from whom.”

Gabriel remained silent longer than ritual permitted. Then he amended the line.

NO REQUEST FOR RESTORATION UNTIL THE SCOPE OF PROTECTION IS DEFINED.

“This sentence will bring the Council upon you.”

“I am here.”

“No.” Gabriel folded the bands of script back into the head of his staff. “You are standing before a door that no longer recognizes you. That is not the same place.”

✦

Lucifer waited in the corridor beyond the Boundary Gate.

He did not lean against a column, fold his arms, or pretend to have wandered there by chance. The light of the Morning Star lay close against his wings, held so tightly that the metal floor reflected only a thin halo beneath his feet.

Michael passed without stopping.

“You have cut your own hand away from the bar,” Lucifer said.

Michael continued for three more steps.

“And named it restraint.”

He stopped.

Healiangel and Gabriel remained behind. The ritual door closed between them, leaving the corridor to the two who had once stood side by side when Heaven had not yet learned that a single command could be heard in two ways.

Michael turned his head. “I did not cut away my hand.”

“Your mark is gone.”

“The hand remains.”

Lucifer looked at Michael’s right hand. “Then when the boundary opens, you will stand there with a hand forbidden to touch it.”

“Perhaps.”

“And if what lies beyond wishes to kill them?”

“I will find a way that does not begin by turning them into things to be locked.”

A smile nearly appeared upon Lucifer’s mouth, but did not take form.

“You have just spoken like me.”

“No.”

“You surrendered power for Humanity’s right to choose.”

“I surrendered a power that could no longer distinguish protection from possession.”

“That is merely a longer way of saying the same thing.”

Michael stepped closer. No sword stood between them, yet his weight still made the light along the walls straighten.

“Do not mistake this decision for agreement, Samael.”

The first name fell into the corridor like a piece of metal laid upon an ancient altar.

Lucifer did not smile.

Michael continued, “Freedom does not erase the responsibility of the stronger. It makes that responsibility heavier.”

“Because the stronger must stand still?”

“Because the stronger must know when his presence has already become a command, even without words.”

The gold in Lucifer’s eyes narrowed.

“Did you learn that from me?”

“I learned it by watching you fail to learn it soon enough.”

Lucifer turned toward the sealed door. “And now you believe Heaven will respect the space you have left behind?”

“No.”

The answer made him look back.

Michael laid the hand that no longer bore authority against his breastplate. “I know only that the space must exist before anyone can choose not to enter it.”

He walked away.

Lucifer remained before the Boundary Gate. Beyond the metal, no image of Humanity opened for him. His name was still removed from all active paths. The seventh slab did not glow.

For the first time, a door of Heaven had closed before him not because Michael held a sword outside it.

It had closed because Michael had withdrawn his hand from the bar.

✦

Adam called once, then sat down before the door.

The sun had risen beyond Eden’s two white pillars. Light slid across the ridge, touched the roof of Lilith’s shelter, and stopped upon the woven mat that had been removed from its frame. The crossbar lay on the ground. Two coils of rope had been wound and set aside. The stones that held the roof were arranged in a low row beside the path.

Nothing had been broken.

Everything had been taken apart by hands that knew exactly how it had once been built.

Adam placed the basket of fruit beside his feet. His half of the bark rested in the hide pouch at his waist, no longer in the outer slot of the door.

“Lilith.”

No answer came.

He did not call a second time.

Wind passed through the empty frame. Once, he would have entered because the way stood open. Later he had learned that an unobstructed passage was not always an invitation.

He waited.

A small bird landed upon a low branch, pecked at a length of cord, and flew away. The shadows of the two white pillars behind him shortened. When Adam began to think Lilith had left before dawn, the sound of stone striking stone came from the upper slope.

Lilith appeared carrying a bundle of branches across one shoulder and a black stone pressed against her hip. Her hair was tied back with new cord. The burn in her palm had faded to a red line.

She looked at Adam, then at the distance he had kept before the empty frame.

“You called.”

“I waited.”

Lilith set down the branches. “I saw.”

Adam pointed to the shelter. “Repair?”

“Leave.”

He looked at the stacked stones, the wound rope, the mat removed from the frame. “Rain coming?”

“No.”

“Beasts?”

“No.”

“Place broken?”

Lilith turned toward the white pillars. From the shelter they remained plainly visible between the trees—high, white, and still, like two fingers of a colossal hand laid upon the horizon.

“This place sees Eden.”

Adam did not understand. “Good. See path.”

“Every day, see path.”

“Not lost.”

“Every choice looks back there.”

She pointed to the pillars, then to the shelter. “Here is outside Eden. But still Eden’s outside.”

Adam looked at the ground they had cleared, the fire ring, the branch roof, the two-sided door. All of it had been made from stone, reeds, vines, and their hands. None belonged more to the garden than to the hillside. Yet he understood what Lilith meant in a way that made his chest grow heavy.

The shelter was defined by what it stood beyond.

“Where go?”

Lilith pointed north toward the dark ridges, where the land rose into three stone backs and hid the horizon. “Beyond there.”

“No water seen.”

“Birds fly that way at morning.”

“No path.”

“I make one.”

Adam stood. “I come with you.”

Lilith looked at him.

He corrected himself before she had to. “I carry to first ridge.”

She bent and gave him the coil of rope and two flat stones. She did not give him the bundle of branches. She did not give him the black stone. She did not give him the half-piece of bark bound beneath the cloth at her chest.

Adam accepted the part she had chosen.

They left the shelter when the sun stood near its height.

✦

The road had no shape until they stepped upon it.

Lilith went first through the low grass, avoiding patches of soft earth that still held the old rain. Adam followed, arranging pairs of stones wherever the route changed direction. At the third pair, Lilith turned.

“Mark for Eden?”

“Mark for water, shelter.”

“Old shelter.”

Adam looked at the two stones. “To return.”

Lilith lifted one and placed it toward a cleft where the plants grew greener. “To know water.”

She did not erase the sign. She only changed its meaning.

They continued.

At the first ridge the wind strengthened. Eden remained visible behind them, but the two white pillars had diminished to streaks of light among the trees. Adam stopped.

“First ridge.”

Lilith looked at the rope in his hands.

He did not put it down.

“I carry beyond the slope,” Adam said.

“You said first ridge.”

“This ridge not finished.”

Lilith looked at the ground behind them, then at the steep stone ahead. A sound almost like laughter left her through her nose. Not mockery. Not quite joy. Only the sound of someone realizing that words could be bent without being broken.

“Beyond the whole slope.”

They climbed.

At the second ridge, Adam slipped upon loose gravel. The rope fell from his shoulder and rolled into a narrow cleft. Lilith lay flat against the rock and reached down for it. Adam held her ankle. When her fingers caught the coil, gravel broke beneath her chest and slid away with a long dry rattle.

Adam pulled her up too quickly.

Lilith braced a hand against his shoulder, holding space between them before both lost balance.

They sat upon a slab of stone.

“Danger,” Adam said.

“Yes.”

“Turn back.”

“No.”

He pointed down into the cleft. “Death.”

Lilith looked at the hand that still held her ankle. Adam released her at once.

“In Eden, death?” she asked.

Adam shook his head.

“Then outside Eden, living means choosing not to die?”

He frowned. “Living is living.”

“No.” Lilith touched the red line across her palm. “Out here, living is doing many things so death does not come yet.”

Adam looked toward the ridges ahead. “Why choose hard?”

“Because easy chose me first.”

The words silenced him.

Eden had water before they thirsted, fruit before they hungered, leaves before rain, paths of light before they knew how to be lost. Nothing was wrong with such abundance. But because nothing needed to be asked, they had taken so long to learn that they could answer differently.

Adam picked up the rope.

“I carry to the end of the slope.”

Lilith rose. “To the end.”

They went on.

When they reached the third ridge, Eden disappeared.

There was no rite. No light closing behind them. Only one step by Lilith across the stone, and the last treetops sank beyond the land. The two white pillars vanished from the horizon.

Adam stopped in mid-step.

He turned back.

There was nothing but rock, grass, and sky.

“Eden.”

Lilith looked ahead.

The land beyond the ridge opened into a dry high plain scattered with black stones like the spines of a colossal beast beneath the earth. Farther away, low trees gathered around a hollow. Birds descended there and did not immediately rise.

“Water,” she said.

Adam still looked behind them. “No path seen.”

Lilith placed a pair of stones at the crest. One pointed toward the low trees. The other lay sideways, pointing neither toward Eden nor ahead.

“The road is beneath our feet.”

“When dark?”

“Fire.”

“When rain?”

“Roof.”

“When beasts come?”

“Door.”

“When alone?”

Lilith looked at him.

For the first time that day, she did not answer at once.

“I will know.”

It was not certainty. Not defiance. Only a sentence without proof, spoken by someone who knew she would have to pay to learn whether it was true.

Adam set down the rope.

“I go farther with you.”

“You must return before dark.”

“I stay.”

“No.”

The sound no longer made him retreat because he had been rejected. It made him stop because he understood a boundary.

“I help build.”

“Another day, if I call.”

“Tomorrow?”

“I do not know.”

Adam looked across the empty land. “You stay here?”

“I stay outside Eden.”

“Old place also outside.”

“The old place was a door.” Lilith placed a hand upon her chest. “This place is a road.”

He understood more slowly than she did, but not less fully.

The first shelter had allowed Lilith to prove she could live beyond the garden. Yet each morning the two white pillars still stood within her sight. Every return of Adam began from a place already given. She did not want to spend her life merely standing beyond a boundary made by someone else.

She wanted a direction that had not been created only to lead away.

Adam opened the hide pouch at his waist and drew out his half of the bark. The wood had darkened with sweat and water. Both signs remained clear.

Together.

Not speaking for.

He held it out.

Lilith did not take it.

“Your part.”

Adam closed his hand around the bark. “Road remains?”

“Yes.”

“You return?”

“Perhaps.”

“Stay in Eden?”

Lilith shook her head.

It was the first time the decision had been spoken clearly enough that neither could pretend tomorrow would restore what had been.

Adam lowered his head. Not long. Only long enough for breath to pass through pain before pain became a command.

“I want you to return.”

“I know.”

“I do not want to be alone.”

Lilith looked at him. The sky behind Adam held no white pillars to keep the horizon straight. He was only a person standing in a wide land, carrying a fear with nowhere to hide.

She stepped close and placed her forehead against his.

Not a promise to return.

Not consent to remain.

Only a way for one person’s pain not to become the cord around another.

“You are not no one,” she said.

Adam closed his eyes.

“But no longer in the same place.”

“No.”

When they drew apart, he pressed his half of the bark to his chest, then raised it for her to see. Lilith made the same gesture with her own.

The two halves no longer rested upon one threshold.

Both signs remained whole.

Adam turned back.

For the first time, he left Lilith without knowing exactly when he would see her again.

✦

The warning appeared in Heaven when Eden vanished from Adam’s sight.

No bell. No image. Only a thin band of light crossed Gabriel’s record-table and stopped at the edge of the observation range.

ONE HUMAN LIFE-RHYTHM HAS MOVED BEYOND THE CURRENT ROUTING RANGE.

Gabriel called Michael by habit.

The summons reached the Boundary Gate and died.

He looked at the empty place where Michael’s response had once appeared.

Healiangel arrived before Michael.

“Direct danger?” he asked.

“No.”

“Injury?”

“No.”

“External agent?”

“None recorded.”

“Then this is movement.”

“Beyond range.”

“Whose range?”

Gabriel did not answer.

Michael entered. He read the warning, then placed a hand upon the record-table. No image opened.

Gabriel said, “If your authority still held, we could compel a frame of sight and confirm her location.”

“I know.”

“Do you revise your request concerning restoration?”

Michael read the three lines again.

No danger.

No injury.

No external agent.

“No.”

Gabriel tightened his grip on the staff. “What if she disappears?”

“She has not disappeared.”

“We cannot see her.”

Michael looked at him. “Those are not the same sentence.”

A golden light appeared at the threshold of the Archive.

Lucifer did not enter the recording circle. He stood exactly where the restrictions permitted.

“Open it for me,” he said.

Michael did not turn. “No.”

“You cannot.”

“That as well.”

Lucifer looked at the warning. “I need only know that she lives.”

Healiangel answered, “The data has already said so.”

“The data says a life-rhythm has gone beyond the place where you know how to follow it.”

“Yes.”

“And you find that sufficient?”

Healiangel looked at him. “No. But not knowing does not grant the right to look unseen.”

Lucifer opened his mouth, then stopped.

Behind him, the seventh slab remained dark. No path bore his name. No surface of water returned his face. If Lilith had gone where Eden was no longer visible, he too had lost the prepared surface through which he might appear.

The light around his wings lowered.

“Then record it correctly,” Lucifer said.

Gabriel looked at him. “Correctly how?”

“Not missing.”

Michael turned.

For one beat, the two looked at each other as though both had reached the same sentence from opposite sides.

Gabriel placed the tip of his staff upon the record-table.

“Then what is she?”

Michael answered, “Gone by her own leaving.”

Gabriel wrote.

LILITH: DEPARTED EDEN’S RANGE BY HER OWN MOVEMENT.

He paused. “Status of return?”

Michael looked at the minimum warning that still glowed.

“The road is not closed.”

Healiangel said, “But it is not to be presumed.”

Gabriel added the final line.

ROAD OF RETURN: OPEN. NOT ASSUMED.

The band of light at the edge of the observation range went dark.

No one asked to reopen it.

✦

Adam reached the first ridge as the sun touched the horizon.

From there, the two white pillars appeared again.

He stood watching them until his shadow stretched across the road he had just walked. Beyond the three ridges, Lilith was somewhere Eden could not be seen. Ahead, the garden remained open as though nothing had changed.

Adam descended.

When he passed the old shelter, he stopped before the empty frame. The mat was gone. The crossbar had been carried away. Wind passed through without anyone’s permission.

He laid a hand upon one wooden post.

He did not pull it down.

He did not rebuild it.

He let it stand as proof that a place once called home need not remain home forever.

Then he returned to Eden.

Beyond the three ridges, Lilith found water near nightfall.

A narrow spring ran between black stones, cold and clear, without the song of the river in the garden. She knelt and drank. The water tasted of metal and earth. It was not sweet. It had not been prepared for her.

She drank a second time.

Lilith set the bundle of branches beneath an overhang, bound the rope into a low roof, and struck black stone against dry fiber. The fire did not catch at once. She tried again. On the third attempt, a spark took the grass and spread into the smaller branches.

No light fell from Heaven to aid her.

No water opened into the Archive.

No door stood behind her.

Lilith placed her half of the bark beside the fire.

Together.

Not speaking for.

The signs did not command her to return. Neither did they command her to forget the one who held the other half.

Night descended upon a land without a name.

Eden still existed beyond the three ridges. But from that night onward, it was no longer the place Lilith was leaving.

It was only a place where she had once lived.

— END OF CHAPTER 13 —
content_vi:
Dấu kiếm biến mất trước khi ánh sáng quanh nó kịp nguội.

Michael đứng trước Cổng Giới Tuyến, bàn tay phải mở trên mặt phiến kim loại từng nhận quyền của chàng. Những đường khắc vẫn còn đó: bảy vòng lồng vào nhau, một trục thẳng đi qua giữa, dấu của kẻ được phép mở đường khi hai cõi chạm quá gần. Nhưng ánh sáng đã rời khỏi chúng. Phiến kim loại không tối đi; nó chỉ không còn nhận ra chàng.

Gabriel đứng phía bên kia vòng nghi thức, trượng dựng thẳng trước ngực. Ba dải văn tự chạy quanh đầu trượng, chậm và đều như những lưỡi dao chưa quyết định sẽ hạ xuống nơi nào.

Healiangel ở giữa họ.

Không ai yêu cầu anh đứng ở đó.

Michael đặt ngón tay lên vòng ngoài cùng. Không phản hồi.

“Xác nhận lần cuối,” Gabriel nói. “Quyền giới tuyến của ngươi đã được rút khỏi toàn bộ nhánh hồ sơ Nhân Loại. Quyền mở sâu, cưỡng hình ảnh, ép hồi đáp và đóng phản hồi đều không còn nhận dấu của ngươi.”

“Ta biết.”

“Ngươi không thể tự phục hồi.”

“Ta biết.”

“Hội Đồng hỏi ngươi có yêu cầu mở nghi thức hoàn nguyên hay không.”

Michael nhìn phiến kim loại. Một vết lõm rất nhỏ còn in nơi chàng đã đặt lưỡi kiếm lên dấu quyền hạn. Không phải vết nứt. Không phải tổn thương. Chỉ là bằng chứng rằng một quyền lực từng nằm ở đó đã được lấy đi bằng chính bàn tay mang nó.

“Không.”

Ba dải văn tự quanh trượng Gabriel dừng lại cùng lúc.

“Nếu không có yêu cầu hoàn nguyên, nhánh Nhân Loại sẽ không có người giữ giới tuyến đơn phương.”

“Nó vẫn có cảnh báo nguy hiểm tối thiểu.”

“Cảnh báo không phải hành động.”

“Hành động không phải lúc nào cũng là quyền.”

Gabriel nhìn thẳng vào chàng. “Khi điều gì đó đi qua mà chúng ta không thể đóng, câu ấy sẽ không giữ được ai.”

Michael khép bàn tay.

“Khi điều đó xảy ra, ta sẽ chịu phần của mình.”

“Ngươi vừa bỏ công cụ giúp ngươi tránh phần ấy.”

“Không.” Michael quay khỏi phiến kim loại. “Ta bỏ công cụ cho phép ta bắt kẻ khác chịu thay.”

Khoảng thiếu dưới cánh trái Healiangel siết lại. Anh đã cảm thấy đường nối đi xuống im đi từ lúc nghi thức kết thúc, nhưng không biến mất. Nó vẫn tồn tại như một hình dạng được nhớ trong bản thể, không sáng, không gọi, không dẫn đến bất kỳ nơi nào anh có quyền đặt tên.

Gabriel hạ trượng.

“Ta sẽ ghi: từ chối hoàn nguyên.”

“Ghi điều đã xảy ra.”

“Đó là điều đã xảy ra.”

“Không.” Michael nhìn ngài. “Ta không từ chối trách nhiệm. Ta từ chối lấy lại quyền ấy trước khi Thiên Đàng biết nó đang bảo vệ ai khỏi ai.”

Gabriel im lặng lâu hơn một nhịp nghi lễ cho phép. Sau đó ngài sửa dòng chữ.

KHÔNG YÊU CẦU HOÀN NGUYÊN TRƯỚC KHI PHẠM VI BẢO HỘ ĐƯỢC XÁC ĐỊNH.

“Câu này sẽ khiến Hội Đồng gọi ngươi đến.”

“Ta đang ở đây.”

“Không.” Gabriel cuộn những dải văn tự vào đầu trượng. “Ngươi đang đứng trước một cánh cửa không còn nhận ngươi. Đó không phải cùng một nơi.”

✦

Lucifer chờ ở hành lang ngoài Cổng Giới Tuyến.

Y không dựa vào cột, không khoanh tay, không làm ra vẻ tình cờ đi ngang. Ánh sáng của Sao Mai nằm sát đôi cánh, được giữ gọn đến mức sàn kim loại chỉ phản lại một quầng mỏng dưới chân y.

Michael đi qua mà không dừng.

“Ngươi đã cắt tay mình khỏi then cài,” Lucifer nói.

Michael tiếp tục thêm ba bước.

“Và gọi đó là tiết chế.”

Chàng dừng lại.

Healiangel và Gabriel còn ở phía sau. Cánh cửa nghi thức khép giữa họ, để hành lang chỉ còn hai người đã từng đứng cạnh nhau khi Thiên Đàng chưa biết một mệnh lệnh có thể được nghe theo hai cách.

Michael quay đầu. “Ta không cắt tay mình.”

“Dấu của ngươi biến mất.”

“Tay vẫn còn.”

Lucifer nhìn bàn tay phải của chàng. “Vậy khi đường biên mở, ngươi sẽ đứng đó với một bàn tay không được phép chạm vào.”

“Có thể.”

“Và nếu thứ ở phía bên kia muốn giết họ?”

“Ta sẽ tìm một cách không bắt đầu bằng việc biến họ thành vật bị khóa.”

Một nụ cười gần như xuất hiện trên môi Lucifer, nhưng không thành hình.

“Ngươi vừa nói như ta.”

“Không.”

“Ngươi từ bỏ quyền lực vì quyền tự quyết của Nhân Loại.”

“Ta từ bỏ một quyền lực không còn phân biệt được bảo vệ với sở hữu.”

“Đó chỉ là cách dài hơn để nói cùng một điều.”

Michael bước đến gần. Không có kiếm giữa họ, nhưng sức nặng của chàng vẫn làm ánh sáng trên tường thẳng lại.

“Đừng nhầm quyết định này với sự đồng thuận, Samael.”

Tên nguyên thủy rơi xuống hành lang như một mảnh kim loại được đặt lên bàn thờ cũ.

Lucifer không cười.

Michael nói tiếp: “Tự do không xóa trách nhiệm của kẻ mạnh hơn. Nó làm trách nhiệm ấy nặng hơn.”

“Vì kẻ mạnh phải đứng yên?”

“Vì kẻ mạnh phải biết khi nào sự hiện diện của mình đã trở thành một mệnh lệnh, dù không nói ra.”

Ánh vàng trong mắt Lucifer thu hẹp.

“Ngươi học điều đó từ ta?”

“Ta học từ việc nhìn ngươi không học đủ sớm.”

Ngoài ba sống đá, Lilith tìm thấy nước khi trời gần tối.

Một mạch nhỏ chảy giữa những phiến đá đen, lạnh và trong, không hát như dòng sông trong khu vườn. Nàng quỳ xuống uống. Nước có vị kim loại và đất. Không ngọt. Không được chuẩn bị cho nàng.

Nàng vẫn uống lần thứ hai.

Lilith đặt bó cành dưới một mỏm đá, buộc dây thành mái thấp và nhóm lửa bằng đá đen cùng sợi khô nàng mang theo. Ngọn lửa không bùng ngay. Nàng thử lại. Lần thứ ba, một tia sáng bắt vào cỏ khô rồi lan sang cành nhỏ.

Không ánh sáng nào từ trời rơi xuống giúp nàng.

Không mặt nước nào mở ra Thư Khố.

Không cánh cửa nào đứng sau lưng.

Lilith lấy nửa mảnh vỏ đặt cạnh ngọn lửa.

Cùng.

Không nói thay.

Hai dấu không bảo nàng phải quay lại. Chúng cũng không bắt nàng quên người đã giữ nửa còn lại.

Đêm xuống trên vùng đất chưa có tên.

Eden vẫn tồn tại ở phía sau ba sống đá. Nhưng từ đêm ấy, nó không còn là nơi Lilith đang rời khỏi.

Nó chỉ là một nơi nàng đã từng sống.

— HẾT CHƯƠNG 13 —
